519: The vowels η and ω are always long; ε and ο are always short, while α, ι and υ are sometimes long and sometimes short.
521: Diphthongs (including improper ones) are always long.
522: A syllable is long by position when its vowel is followed by two or more consonants, or by a double consonant.
524: If a mute, followed by a liquid, comes after a short vowel, and the mute and liquid come within the same word, the syllable may be either long or short according to the requirements of the verse.
526: One of the consonants which make a syllable long by position (particularly ϝ, occasionally σ) is sometimes lost but still pronounced.
537: The circumflex accent can stand only over a long vowel or a diphthong.
544: The antepenult when accented must have the acute, but it cannot have the accent if the last syllable is long by nature or position.
545: An accented penult has the circumflex if it is long by nature while the ultima is short by nature.
586: Two successive vowels which do not form a diphthong are sometimes pronounced as one syllable for the sake of the metre. The two syllables may come in separate words.
1161: If a long penult has the acute accent, then the ultima must be long also.
1162: If the ultima is short and the penult has the acute accent, then the penult must be short also.
1167: If an apparently short final syllable stands where a long is expected, it is probable that the pause of the caesura or diaeresis fills out the time required for the foot.
1168: Short syllables ending in a single consonant are occasionally lengthened in thesis although the next word begins with a vowel.
1169: If a long syllable is followed by a short, then the next syllable must be short also.
1173: When a syllable ends in a long vowel or a diphthong and the next syllable begins with a vowel, the long final vowel or diphthong is regularly shortened.
1184: The final syllable of a verse is always considered long.
